texto:
Google Ads advertisers now have access to an AI campaign localization tool that turns an existing English (US) Search campaign into a separate campaign in one of 10 other languages, according to PPC News Feed, which first reported the tool's availability on October 23, 2026. The tool translates headlines, descriptions, sitelinks, callouts and keywords, strips text out of images, and offers a script that translates landing pages on the fly when a user clicks an ad. It is labelled a beta.
The documentation behind it is a Google Ads Help Center page, About the AI campaign localization tool for Search campaigns (beta), which carries no publication date. PPC News Feed reported on October 5, 2026 that Google had published the page, crediting Dario Zannoni with spotting it. The October 23 report describes the tool as available "within Google Ads," following the help page's publication earlier in the month. According to PPC News Feed, Google Ads coach Jyll Saskin Gales noted that what she called Google's Campaign Translator had become publicly available after a period in which it was offered by request only. Google has not published a dated announcement for the rollout, and the help page does not say which accounts have access.
ELI5
Google built a button in Google Ads that takes an English search ad campaign and makes a copy of it in another language, such as French or Polish, using AI to do the translating. It matters for businesses that want to sell in other countries but have been held back by the cost and time of translating ads by hand. The original campaign stays untouched, but the copy keeps the same budget number without converting the currency, so a person still has to check the money and the wording before switching it on.
What the tool produces
The central design choice is separation. "When you localize a campaign, the system creates a brand new, independent campaign. Your original campaign is never modified," according to the help page. The localized version is therefore a fresh entity in the account, with its own performance history starting from zero.
Google lists four groups of components that the tool handles.
Text assets and targeting. Headlines, descriptions, sitelinks, callouts and keywords are translated into the target language. Keywords are included, which means the targeting layer of the campaign, and not only the ad copy, is converted by the model. The headline assets in a responsive search ad are the most visible part of that output, but the keyword translations decide which queries the new campaign enters auctions for.
Images. Where images carry text overlays, "the AI will remove the text (in-paint) to provide a clean image, and add the translated messaging as supplemental text assets," according to Google. The tool does not redraw translated words onto the image. It deletes the original lettering and moves the message into separate text assets.
Landing pages. Advertisers can embed a JavaScript snippet supplied by Google, which translates the text on the landing page when a user arrives from an ad. The alternative is to update URLs by hand or apply a bulk find-and-replace rule to domains.
Budgets and bids. These are copied exactly. "The system doesn't perform currency conversions or exchange rate calculations. For example, a $100 USD budget becomes a $100 USD budget in the localized campaign," the page states.
That last point is narrower than it looks. The budget figure carries over unchanged, and so do bids, regardless of how cost-per-click levels in the target market compare with those in the source market. A campaign built for the United States and copied into Polish keeps the same numbers. Whether those numbers make sense for a different country, auction and price level is left to the advertiser.
Five steps from campaign to paused draft
Google describes the workflow in five steps.
The first is access, and there are three routes in: selecting an eligible campaign in the Campaigns table and choosing the localization option, opening Localization from the Tools menu, or applying what the help page calls an "Optiscore localization recommendation." Those recommendations "are triggered if Google Ads identifies opportunities to increase performance with localization," according to the page. That places the feature inside the same recommendations system Google uses to promote other automated settings.
The second step sets the campaign name, which is pre-filled from the original, the target language, the new location and the new budget. A free-form field accepts "global instructions." Google's examples are "Do not translate the brand name" and "Keep the tone formal." The help page gives no character limit for this field and does not say how strictly the model follows it. The mechanism resembles the plain-language guidance Google introduced elsewhere this year: AI Brief, announced on April 30, 2026, lets advertisers give AI Max for Search campaigns written instructions about messaging and matching.
The third step is review, and here Google makes an unusual claim. "You don't need prior knowledge of the target language to review your new campaign," according to the page. The review table has four columns: the original asset, the translated asset, a "translation back" into English, and translation notes. The back-translation is meant to let an advertiser check that "the meaning and intent remain accurate." Each translated asset can be edited inline.
Back-translation is an established quality check in the translation trade, but it has limits. A phrase can return to English intact while sounding stilted, wrong in register or legally loaded in the target market. Nothing on the help page addresses idiom, local advertising rules or regulated claims that differ between, for example, Brazil and Portugal, both of which appear as separate targets.
The fourth step is the landing page strategy. Under the AI translation option, "Google provides a code snippet for you to copy and paste to your website, which dynamically translates the texts on the landing page when a user clicks the ad," the page states. Google says the tag only needs to be installed "once per account even if you are running multiple localized campaigns," and points to its documentation on the Google tag. The second option is a bulk domain update using a find-and-replace rule, with the example of changing example.com/en to example.com/fr. The page also lists the line "Do not update any URLs" in this step without further explanation.
The fifth step is publishing. By default, the new campaign is published in a "Paused" state "so you can perform final reviews before it goes live," according to Google.
The landing page script
The landing page option deserves a closer look, because it changes something outside the ad account. A JavaScript snippet that rewrites page text at load time is a new piece of code running on the advertiser's site, in the same family as the site tag that ad platforms already ask sites to carry. The help page does not describe how the translation is served, whether translated text is cached, how it interacts with consent banners, or whether the translated version of the page is visible to search crawlers. It also does not say whether the translated page text is stored or reused by Google.
PPC News Feed's October 5 report noted that the snippet can be deployed through Google Tag Manager. The help page itself refers to the code both as a "provided JavaScript snippet" and as "the Google tag."
For advertisers, the practical gap is between the ad and the page. A localized ad pointing to an English page is a known cause of poor conversion. Google's script attempts to close that gap without the advertiser building translated pages, but the translated page is generated per visit, and the advertiser does not review it in the five-step flow. The review table covers ad assets, not page copy.
Languages, limits and an expired date
The tool supports Search campaigns only. The source language must be English (US). The 10 target languages are:
- Dutch
- French
- French (Canada)
- German
- Italian
- Polish
- Portuguese (Brazil)
- Portuguese (Portugal/European)
- Spanish (Castilian/Spain)
- Spanish (Latin American & Caribbean)
Counted by base language, the list covers seven languages, with regional variants for French, Portuguese and Spanish. No Asian, Nordic or Middle Eastern language is included, and British English is not offered as either a source or a target.
The help page contains a forward-looking note: "Campaign localization will expand to add additional target languages by the end of 2026. Starting September 2026, the tool will support Performance Max campaigns." The page, which still lists Search as the only supported campaign type, makes that statement about a month that has already ended. Neither source document confirms whether Performance Max support has started, and the October 23 report from PPC News Feed describes the tool only in relation to Search.
Eligibility rules are short. The original campaign must be active or paused; removed, draft, experimental and "shadow" campaigns are not supported. The campaign "must not exceed entity size limits," a threshold the page does not quantify. Every asset and keyword in the source campaign must be in the supported source language: "If the campaign contains unsupported languages, it cannot be localized." A US campaign that mixes English and Spanish keywords to reach bilingual users would therefore be excluded.
There is also a political carve-out. "Election-verified customers aren't eligible to use this feature," according to Google, which links that restriction to its disclosure requirements for synthetic or digitally altered content. Google has required election advertisers to disclose synthetic content in political ads since July 2024, and the exclusion keeps AI-edited images and AI-written copy out of that category of advertiser entirely.
Why the timing matters
The tool arrives weeks after Google removed one of the main manual controls for multilingual Search advertising. Google first said in August 2025 that the language targeting setting would be removed from Search campaigns by the end of 2025, to be replaced by automatic detection of the languages users understand. That deadline slipped. On August 14, 2026, Google said it would drop campaign-level language targeting from Search and Performance Max in September 2026, nine months late. In that announcement, Google stated that it "does not translate ad creatives," and that text customization in AI Max generates copy from landing pages and existing assets without translating it.
With language targeting gone, the language of the ad creative and the landing page has become one of the main signals Google uses to decide which users see which ad. That gives advertisers a structural reason to run separate campaigns per language, and the localization tool now produces those campaigns for them. The earlier statement that Google does not translate creatives described ad serving; the new tool sits at the campaign-building stage, where the advertiser triggers the translation and publishes the result.
The approach also differs from what advertisers have reported on Meta. On October 22, 2026, PPC Land covered reports that Meta's AI had been translating ad copy and adding sitelinks in live campaigns without advertisers requesting it, while Meta's revised Commercial Terms, effective October 30, 2026, make advertisers "solely responsible" for changes its AI features make. Google's localization tool, by contrast, is opt-in, writes into a new campaign rather than the existing one, and defaults to a paused state. The help page does not, however, say who carries responsibility for errors in machine-translated ads, nor does it describe how the translated assets are checked against ad policies in each market before serving.
Google has also been widening the scope of automated asset handling in other campaign types. PPC Land reported on October 21, 2026 that newly created Performance Max campaigns will have image extraction switched on by default from December 4, 2026, even where the account-level dynamic images setting is off. The localization tool's in-painting of images, which removes overlaid text, is another case of Google's systems editing advertiser creative, although here the advertiser initiates the change.
What remains unclear
Several questions are not answered by either source. The help page is undated, and Google has issued no announcement giving a rollout date or the share of accounts with access. The beta label means the feature can still change, and the page's own September 2026 commitment for Performance Max has passed without confirmation in the documentation. The page sets no limits on the number of localized campaigns per account, gives no detail on how translated keywords are matched to queries in the target language, and offers no performance data from testers. Google's description of the benefit, "Instead of waiting extended periods for manual translation and spreadsheet uploads, you can use the tool to help translate text, images, targeting, and landing pages with a few clicks," is a statement of speed, not of results.
For advertisers running US English Search campaigns who want to enter Western European or Latin American markets, the tool reduces the setup work to a few screens. The commercial decisions, including budget levels in a different currency environment, bids in a different auction, and whether the translated copy meets local rules, remain with the advertiser.
Timeline
- July 2024 - Google requires election advertisers to disclose synthetic or digitally altered content in political ads
- August 18, 2025 - Google says the language targeting setting will be removed from Search campaigns by the end of 2025
- April 30, 2026 - Google announces AI Brief for plain-language instructions in AI Max for Search
- August 14, 2026 - Google sets September 2026 for removing campaign-level language targeting from Search and Performance Max and says it does not translate ad creatives
- September 2026 - Date by which the help page says the localization tool will support Performance Max; no confirmation found
- October 5, 2026 - PPC News Feed reports that Google has published a help page for the AI campaign localization tool beta
- October 21, 2026 - Google says new Performance Max campaigns will have image extraction on by default from December 4
- October 22, 2026 - Reports surface of Meta AI translating ad copy unrequested, with new terms making advertisers solely responsible from October 30
- October 23, 2026 - PPC News Feed reports that the campaign translation tool is live in Google Ads
- End of 2026 - Google's stated target for adding more target languages
Related PPC Land coverage
- Google Ads drops language targeting in September, nine months past deadline - Google's August 2026 confirmation that campaign-level language targeting would leave Search and Performance Max, with its statement that it does not translate ad creatives.
- Google removes language targeting from Search campaigns by 2025 - The original 2025 plan to replace manual language settings with automatic detection of user languages.
- Meta makes advertisers solely responsible for its AI ad edits from Oct 30 - Agency reports of unrequested AI translations and sitelinks in Meta campaigns, and the terms that shift liability to advertisers.
- Google turns on PMax image extraction by default from December 4 - A change that lets Google pull landing page images into new Performance Max campaigns even when the account setting is off.
- AI Brief: Google lets advertisers steer AI Max in plain language - Google's free-text instruction system for AI Max, a close relative of the localization tool's global instructions field.
- Google strengthens political ad transparency with synthetic content disclosure - The 2024 disclosure policy that underpins the exclusion of election-verified advertisers from the localization tool.
Summary
Who: Google Ads advertisers running Search campaigns written in English (US); election-verified advertisers are excluded. PPC News Feed first reported the tool's availability, and Jyll Saskin Gales noted its move from request-only access.
What: A beta AI campaign localization tool that creates a new, independent copy of a Search campaign in one of 10 target languages, translating text assets and keywords, removing text from images, and offering a JavaScript snippet for on-the-fly landing page translation. Budgets and bids are copied without currency conversion, and new campaigns publish paused by default.
When: PPC News Feed reported the help page on October 5, 2026 and the tool's availability in Google Ads on October 23, 2026. The help page is undated, promised Performance Max support from September 2026, and targets more languages by the end of 2026.
Where: Inside the Google Ads interface, through the Campaigns table, the Tools menu or an optimization recommendation, with target markets covering Dutch, French, German, Italian, Polish, Portuguese and Spanish variants.
Why: Google presents the tool as a faster route to new markets than manual translation and spreadsheet uploads. It arrives after Google removed campaign-level language targeting from Search and Performance Max, which made the language of ads and landing pages a primary signal for which users see which ad.
